info.text: Four questions on Primer 4: == against =, combining conditions in filter(), group_by() with summarise(), and what the verbs do to the original table. Unlimited attempts, immediate feedback, zero weight.

name.text: P4Q1 One equals sign or two

questiontext.text:
You want the students in the 2024 batch and write:

students |> filter(batch = 2024)

R refuses. What is wrong?

generalfeedback.text: == asks a question; = assigns a value. filter() needs a question, so it must be filter(batch == 2024). This is one of the two or three most common beginner errors in R, and dplyr's error message says so almost in those words.

answer.text: Comparison needs ==; a single = assigns rather than asks

feedback.text: Not in this dataset. read_csv() read batch as a number, so 2024 is written without quotation marks. Worth checking with glimpse() though: <dbl> means no quotation marks, <chr> means quotation marks.

answer.text: filter() works on columns, so this should be select()

feedback.text: The other way round: filter() keeps rows, select() keeps columns. Keeping only some students is a row operation.

answer.text: The pipe is wrong; it should be students + filter(...)

feedback.text: No. |> is right between verbs; + belongs only in ggplot2, between plot layers. Primer 5 covers that distinction.

generalfeedback.text: A comma inside filter() means and: a row is kept only if every condition holds. If you want or, you have to say so explicitly with |, as in filter(batch == 2024 | attendance_pct > 85), and those two questions have very different answers, so it is worth being deliberate about which you meant.

answer.text: Students who are in the 2024 batch and have attendance above 85
Students who are in the 2024 batch or have attendance above 85

feedback.text: A comma is and, not or. For or you need the vertical bar: filter(batch == 2024 | attendance_pct > 85), which here would return far more students.
That would be select(batch, attendance_pct). filter() never changes which columns you have: it only decides which rows survive, and all 17 columns come back.

answer.text: An error, because filter() takes only one condition

feedback.text: It takes as many as you like, separated by commas. Splitting a complicated condition across several commas is usually easier to read than joining them with &.

questiontext.text:
You want one row per teaching_arm, showing the number of students and their mean posttest score. Eleven of the 240 students have no post-test score.

Which of these gives you what you asked for?

generalfeedback.text: group_by() then summarise(), with na.rm = TRUE so the eleven students without a post-test do not turn both means into NA. Always report n beside a mean: your reader needs to know whether it rests on 8 students or 80, and here the two routes to the answer (excluding inside mean(), or dropping those rows first) leave you with different n, so the number is not decoration.

answer.text:
students |>
  group_by(teaching_arm) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_posttest = mean(posttest, na.rm = TRUE))

feedback.text: Correct, 76.4 in the flipped arm against 70.7 in the traditional one.
So close. The shape is right, but mean_posttest comes back as NA for both arms: eleven students have no post-test score, and the mean of anything containing NA is NA. Add na.rm = TRUE inside mean().

answer.text:
students |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_posttest = mean(posttest, na.rm = TRUE))

feedback.text: This gives one row for the whole cohort, not one per arm, which hides the very comparison you wanted. summarise() collapses everything unless group_by() has told it what the groups are.

answer.text:
students |>
  filter(teaching_arm) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_posttest = mean(posttest, na.rm = TRUE))

feedback.text: filter() needs a condition, something that is TRUE or FALSE, and a column of text is neither, so this stops with an error. Splitting a table into groups is group_by()'s job, not filter()'s.

name.text: P4Q4 The verbs do not edit your table

questiontext.text:
You run this and look at the result:

students |>
  filter(batch == 2024) |>
  arrange(desc(attendance_pct))

Afterwards, the object students contains only the 2024 batch.

generalfeedback.text: False. dplyr verbs return a new table and leave the original untouched, so you can experiment freely without damaging your data. The flip side is that a result you want to keep must be assigned to a name: students_2024 <- students |> filter(batch == 2024). Beginners lose an afternoon to each half of this in turn.

feedback.text: No, the verbs never edit the table you started from. students still holds all 240 rows; the filtered version was printed and then discarded, because it was not assigned to anything.
Correct. students is unchanged, which is also why you must assign the result if you want to keep it.
